clinicalPearls: Rare, severe chronic malabsorptive enteropathy defined histologically by an abnormally thickened subepithelial collagen band with villous atrophy in the small bowel.
Presents with chronic watery diarrhoea, progressive weight loss, malabsorption and features of nutritional deficiency.
Strong association with coeliac disease, and it frequently arises in refractory coeliac disease that no longer responds to a gluten-free diet.
May coexist with collagenous colitis and collagenous gastritis as part of a wider collagenous gastroenteritides spectrum.
A drug association, especially with olmesartan and other angiotensin receptor blockers, can produce a sprue-like enteropathy with collagen deposition, so the medication history must be reviewed.
Diagnosis rests on small-bowel biopsy, with the subepithelial collagen band highlighted on trichrome staining and often entrapping capillaries and inflammatory cells.
Congo red staining is negative, which distinguishes the collagen band from amyloid.
Frequently unresponsive to gluten withdrawal alone, so many patients require corticosteroids or immunosuppression together with nutritional support.
reference.pathophysiology: Collagenous sprue is characterised by deposition of a thickened band of collagen beneath the surface epithelium of the small intestine, accompanied by variable villous atrophy, intraepithelial lymphocytosis and lamina propria inflammation. The band is composed predominantly of disorganised collagen with entrapped capillaries and an irregular interface with the overlying epithelium, which is often detached or atrophic. The prevailing mechanism is chronic mucosal injury with dysregulated repair, in which activated subepithelial myofibroblasts lay down excess extracellular matrix. It is frequently linked to gluten-sensitive enteropathy and appears to represent a shared histological endpoint of several chronic injurious processes, including coeliac disease, autoimmune enteropathy and drug injury such as that from olmesartan. The collagen band and epithelial disruption impair absorptive surface function, producing the severe malabsorption that characterises the condition.
additionalDifferentials: Coeliac disease and refractory coeliac disease (types I and II)
Olmesartan and other drug-induced sprue-like enteropathy
Tropical sprue and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
Gastrointestinal amyloidosis (the collagen band being distinguished by negative Congo red staining)
additionalInvestigations: Duodenal and jejunal biopsies with collagen-specific stains (Masson trichrome) and Congo red to exclude amyloid
Coeliac serology (anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies) and HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing
T-cell receptor clonality and intraepithelial lymphocyte immunophenotyping to assess for refractory coeliac disease and lymphoma
Nutritional panel including iron studies, folate, vitamin B12, fat-soluble vitamins, calcium, magnesium and albumin
Medication review with a trial of drug withdrawal where a culprit such as olmesartan is identified
Cross-sectional imaging, capsule endoscopy or enteroscopy to assess extent and exclude lymphoma
Faecal studies to exclude infection and to assess the degree of malabsorption
redFlags: Severe dehydration, electrolyte derangement and marked weight loss from intractable diarrhoea
Features suggesting enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma such as fever, night sweats, an abdominal mass, obstruction or perforation
Refractoriness to both a gluten-free diet and corticosteroids
Profound nutritional deficiency requiring parenteral nutrition
reference.prognosis: Historically regarded as having a poor outlook, but the prognosis has improved with recognition and treatment; many patients respond to a gluten-free diet with corticosteroids or immunosuppression and nutritional support, although a subset progress to refractory disease or lymphoma or require long-term parenteral nutrition.
pitfalls: Attributing non-response to a gluten-free diet solely to dietary non-adherence and missing collagenous sprue.
Overlooking drug causes, particularly olmesartan, which may be reversible on withdrawal.
Failing to distinguish the collagen band from amyloid or from a normally thickened basement membrane.
Missing an underlying or emerging enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma.
Relying on superficial biopsies that miss the subepithelial collagen band and lead to a missed diagnosis.
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease (standard reference)
Morson and Dawson's Gastrointestinal Pathology (standard reference)
Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (standard reference)
